title: Short Stuff: Is It Theater or Theatre?
summary: Short Stuff episode on why "theater" is spelled two ways (theatre with -re vs. theater with -er). Josh and Chuck open with tour-venue anecdotes about signage spelling, then trace the split to Noah Webster: his American Spelling Book (the Blue-Backed Speller), which sold a huge number of copies and helped standardize American English, and his American Dictionary of the English Language, which pushed American spellings like color, honor, plow, and draft. They note Webster's failed proposals (tongue, women) and the informal convention that the industry uses -re while venues use -er, but agree either spelling is understood and usage is mostly descriptive. Ends with a short sign-off.
topics: American Dictionary of the English Language

segments.title: Theatre vs. theater spelling intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic: why some venues spell theater with -re and others with -er. He and Chuck discuss tour venues and billboard aesthetics, joking about how the -re spelling looks more regal.

segments.title: Noah Webster's background
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Noah Webster as the American dictionary maker, not the Oxford English Dictionary author, and describe his birth in Connecticut in 1758, his Yale education, his Revolutionary-era militia service, his work as a teacher and attorney, and his antislavery society and Amherst College involvement.
topics: Connecticut Society for the Abolition of Slavery

segments.title: Webster's American Spelling Book
segments.summary: Webster wanted American schoolchildren to stop learning from British books. His American Spelling Book, called the Blue-Backed Speller, sold a very large number of copies and remained in print, helping standardize American English for teachers.

segments.title: American Dictionary and spelling changes
segments.summary: Webster next produced the American Dictionary of the English Language, about 70,000 words. It promoted American spellings such as color, honor, plow, and draft. Some proposals, like tongue and women, did not stick.
topics: American Dictionary of the English Language

segments.title: Theater spelling conventions and outro
segments.summary: The hosts explain that theater was previously spelled only with -re before Webster. They note a notion that the theater industry uses -re while venues use -er, but agree that either spelling is understood and language is descriptive. Brief sign-off follows.
